messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh, a 57-year-old interior designer of Vietnamese heritage, had been running a pop-up design booth at a weekend market when a terrorist bomb detonated near the food vendors. The blast threw her against a concrete pillar; she remembers the sharp, sweet smell of spilled rum from a toppled cart mixing with the metallic scent of blood. That olfactory memory has become a powerful trigger: the whiff of alcohol—from a friend’s glass of wine, a cleaning product, even hand sanitizer—suddenly plunges her back into the chaos. Old photographs of the market district, or a casual conversation about that day, also flood her with intrusive images.

When a trigger strikes, Linh feels an urgent need to release the building pressure. She has excused herself to the bathroom and scratched her arm until she felt pain, a self-harm that momentarily grounds her. Other times she binge-eats, or pushes herself through a punishing run, trying to distract and exhaust herself. She is convinced she cannot handle even the slightest upset; the world feels fundamentally dangerous. This low-coping self-view means that when a trigger arises, she never considers other options—her immediate recourse is the same self-harm or overeating, because she believes she lacks the strength to cope differently.

Her hypervigilance and conviction that danger lurks everywhere also intensify her threat responses. She constantly scans her surroundings, watching strangers for signs of hostility. This vigilance primes her to startle violently when a colleague taps her shoulder; her heart races and she feels momentarily back in the market. Because she sees the world as a threat, she interprets ambiguous cues—a quick movement, a sudden scent—as imminent danger, which in turn triggers trauma memories more often. Each flashback leaves her breathless, acting as if the bombing were happening again, and that terror drives her to eat compulsively or exercise until her legs shake.

After each startle or flashback, Linh’s thoughts spiral: “See, I can’t handle anything—the world is not safe.” The threat responses deepen her negative appraisals, and the vivid memories themselves make the alcohol smell more salient in her mind, so she notices it everywhere. Her maladaptive strategies also turn against her. After a binge she feels ashamed, more convinced of her own brokenness; self-harm leaves her feeling estranged from herself, reinforcing her low-coping self-image. The distraction of overeating eventually fades, and the mental void allows trauma memories to rush back. Compulsive exercise leaves her physically depleted yet mentally hyperaroused, triggering intrusive images of the bombing. And when she hurts herself, she becomes frightened of her own impulses, monitoring herself for loss of control—this vigilance heightens her sense of threat, making her even more jumpy at unexpected sounds or touches.

Linh works from a home office now, avoiding client meetings in public spaces. She declined a commission to redesign a community market, citing creative differences. Her marriage has grown tense; she cannot bear her husband’s casual touch at night, and she has hidden the self-harm marks. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment last week when, during a routine traffic stop, the officer’s radio crackled and she smelled coffee—a scent that had not triggered her before—and she dissociated so completely that she could not answer basic questions. She is terrified that she is losing control of her own mind, but part of her also whispers that maybe, just maybe, a therapist can show her a different way to live.
